title: Claude Sonnet 4.6 Cost Teardown: Price the Whole Workload
dek: Sonnet 4.6’s listed token rates are only the starting point. Repeated context, generated text, cache expiry, tool schemas and avoidable calls determine the bill engineers actually operate.
by: Draft for team review · written by a language model from engineers' public reports · checked in code
lead: Claude Sonnet 4.6 is listed at $3.00 per million input tokens, $15.00 per million output tokens and $0.30 per million cached input tokens, with a 1,000,000-token advertised context. The workload bill also reflects repeated output returned as input, cache rewrites after expiry or configuration changes, and large tool schemas; constrain context, keep stable sessions cacheable, and route simple tasks to cheaper models where evaluation supports it.
decisions: Budget input, output, cache reads and cache writes as separate workload categories.
Preserve stable prompt prefixes and configuration when cache reuse matters.
Expose fewer, more distinct tool schemas rather than loading every available server.
Measure retry causes and accepted-work cost instead of counting successful calls alone.
Use Haiku or a decision model for suitable narrow tasks; keep Sonnet for work that earns its cost.

items.mechanism: A large GitHub tool server is roughly 18,000 tokens, and full schemas can be injected on every request.
items.lever: Inspect and narrow exposed tools and connected servers.

items.mechanism: Each repeated call can resend input and generate further output; a workload-specific retry rate is not established.
items.lever: Bound retries and eliminate recurring validation failures.

items.lever: Set effort and tool configuration before cache-sensitive work and avoid unnecessary toggles.

body: The base rate establishes the floor: Claude Sonnet 4.6 is listed at $3.00 per million input tokens and $15.00 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.30 per million. The advertised context is 1,000,000 tokens, but capacity is not a cost target. The direct lever is to send only the context needed for the task and to measure input, output and cached input separately rather than treating a long context window as free storage.

Output is the expensive side of the token mix: a practitioner’s pricing breakdown gives input tokens a 1× base cost and output tokens a 5× base cost. Generated text also returns as input on the next turn, so verbose answers can create a continuing cost surface across a session. The useful lever is response discipline: request compact artifacts, avoid repeating material already present, and stop multi-turn agents once they have delivered the required result rather than inviting ornamental explanation.

Task fit matters because a higher-priced call is not automatically a better outcome. One personal retrieval bot used 8 relevant past replies and reported «Total runtime cost: ~$0.005 per reply.» That is a workload-specific figure, not a transferable Sonnet tariff: retrieval, prompt size and response length shape it. For high-volume classification, a measured cheaper decision model may be a better route; reserve Sonnet 4.6 for tasks whose synthesis or instruction-following quality earns the difference.

body.text: Cache writes, expiry and configuration churn

body: Caching changes the marginal price of repeated stable context: the registry lists cached input at $0.30 per million tokens versus $3.00 for fresh input. A Claude Code pricing account describes cache reads at 0.1× base and fresh input at 1× base. The lever is not merely enabling caching; it is keeping reusable prefixes stable and inspecting cache-hit and cache-write counts, because a prompt that changes every turn cannot reuse as much of its prior context.

Expiry converts a warm-cache workload into a write event. The pricing account gives a 5-minute cache write at 1.25× base and a 1-hour write at 2.00× base, while both read at 0.1×. It says the cache clock is rolling and that activity resets it. Select a duration around actual interaction gaps, and use usage records to distinguish cache reads from writes; otherwise a quiet interval can hide a costly rewrite behind an apparently unchanged prompt.
The TTL is rolling, not fixed from session start.

Configuration churn can also discard reusable context. The pricing account lists switching models, changing effort level, toggling fast mode, changing MCP connections, plugins, compaction and upgrades as cache-invalidating actions. Its practical lever is operational sequencing: settle model and effort choices before a long session, avoid needless toggles, and batch maintenance changes. A switch for genuine quality or reliability reasons can still be justified, but evaluate the rewrite cost along with the new model’s per-token price.

Tool schemas consume input context before the model can act. A discussion of MCP deployments puts a large GitHub server at roughly 18,000 tokens and warns that each connected server can inject its full schema on every request. The lever is selective exposure: inspect the actual tool list, remove irrelevant tools, and avoid connecting broad servers by default. Schema tokens are paid repeatedly unless stable context is reused through cache.

More tools also create an accuracy trade-off, not just a token charge. The MCP guidance recommends a three-server rule and says tool-selection accuracy falls as near-identical descriptions accumulate. That ceiling is practitioner guidance, not a universal model limit. Engineers should test the specific tool surface, expose distinct roles and measure wrong-tool calls; otherwise savings from fewer schemas may be offset by additional corrective turns or human intervention.
A large server like GitHub runs to roughly 18,000 tokens on its own.

The routing comparison offers a concrete alternative for narrow decisions: on 138 task titles, Sonnet 4.6 took 57 seconds and was priced at $1.20 per 1,000 tasks in that setup, while the decision model Jev was $0.01 per 1,000. The reported Sonnet configuration used about 350 input and 10 output tokens per task. This is not a universal price forecast; it shows why a compact classifier can be routed away from Sonnet when its accuracy meets the requirement.

Retries add work when a call fails validation or returns an unusable result: each rerun can resend context and generate more output. No retry rate or retry-specific price is established, so a production budget should not invent one. Instrument retry counts, classify causes, and cap automatic retries; improve the prompt or validator when the same failure recurs rather than treating repeated generation as free.

Effort configuration has a direct cache consequence: changing effort level forces a full cache rewrite. No effort-tier price or Sonnet 4.6 quality curve is established, so there is no supported basis for claiming that more effort always raises or lowers total cost. Keep effort stable within cache-sensitive work, and compare accepted outcomes, repair calls and review burden when deciding whether a harder task merits a change.

The economic unit is accepted work, not the cheapest isolated completion. One Terraform user reported «working on first try» with Sonnet 4.6 after an unsatisfactory Sonnet 5 attempt that supplied imagined values; those are individual experiences, not a benchmark. Establish task-specific evaluations and route simple triage to Haiku 4.5 at $1.00 input and $5.00 output per million tokens when it meets the bar. The lever is selective routing based on error cost and acceptance, not prestige.
